feature_sentence: Provide secure certificate enrollment using EST over HTTP and TLS
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ1. EST profiles certificate enrollment using CMC/PKI messages over an authenticated and authorized HTTPS channel between a client and an EST server acting between the client and a certification authority. The protocol supports secure transfer of enrollment requests and responses and extensible operations such as CSR-attribute retrieval and server-generated keys.

feature_sentence: Apply the EST terminology and normative requirement conventions
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ2. Interpret normative terms such as MUST, SHOULD, MAY, and related requirement levels according to the referenced standards, and use the EST/PKI terminology defined for certification authorities, trust anchors, clients, servers, CMC, CMP, PKCS#10, HTTPS, and TLS.

feature_sentence: Allow clients to obtain the current CA certificates from the EST server
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ4. Before performing other EST operations, a client can request the current EST CA certificate set. The client must authenticate and authorize the EST server using an applicable trust-anchor strategy before relying on the returned CA material.

feature_sentence: Support initial certificate enrollment for an authenticated and authorized client
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ5. After authenticating and authorizing the EST server, a client can submit an enrollment request to obtain its own certificate. The server authenticates and authorizes the client using supported TLS certificate, previously installed certificate, certificate-less TLS, or other permitted authentication mechanisms.

feature_sentence: Authenticate an EST client with a previously installed third-party certificate
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ6. A client that already holds a certificate issued by a recognized third-party CA can present that certificate during the TLS handshake. The EST server verifies the existing certificate and uses it when deciding whether the enrollment request is authorized.

feature_sentence: Support certificate-less TLS mutual authentication
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ7. The EST client and server can mutually authenticate using an approved certificate-less TLS cipher suite when certificate-based authentication is unavailable or unsuitable.

feature_sentence: Support HTTP Basic or Digest client authentication over TLS
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ8. The EST server may request username/password authentication using HTTP Basic or Digest, particularly when TLS client authentication is unavailable or additional authentication is required by policy. HTTP-based authentication must be performed only over a TLS-protected transport.

feature_sentence: Support renewal and rekeying of an existing client certificate
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ9. A client can submit a re-enrollment request to renew or rekey an existing certificate. It should authenticate with the current certificate when suitable, otherwise another accepted enrollment authentication method may be used, while preserving the required subject identity unless a name change is explicitly requested.

feature_sentence: Allow a client to request a server-generated certificate and key pair
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ10. The EST protocol supports a server-key-generation operation in which the client asks the EST server to generate the certificate and associated key pair.

feature_sentence: Transport Full PKI Request messages through the EST Full CMC operation
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ11. EST can carry Full PKI Request messages using the Full CMC Request function, providing access to CMC capabilities that are not available through the simpler enrollment operations.

feature_sentence: Implement EST as a layered protocol using PKI messages, HTTP, and TLS
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ13. EST is structured in layers: PKI/CMC message formats provide enrollment semantics and proof-of-possession, HTTP provides operation URIs, headers, media types, and error signaling, and TLS provides authentication, integrity, confidentiality, and channel-binding information.

feature_sentence: Provide the required EST client application-layer capabilities and configuration
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ14. The client must generate and parse Simple PKI messages, request and parse CA certificates, and support the required trust-anchor configuration. CSR-attribute and Full PKI support may be optional, and the client must be configurable with sufficient server URI information and explicit trust anchors while allowing implicit trust-anchor use to be disabled.

feature_sentence: Use HTTP to transport EST messages and support authentication signaling
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ15. HTTP carries EST request and response messages using operation-specific URIs and registered media types. HTTP authentication can supplement or replace TLS client-certificate authentication when permitted, and persistent HTTP connections may be used.

feature_sentence: Use HTTP status, content type, and redirection rules to control EST operations
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ16. HTTP status codes communicate operation success or failure and Content-Type identifies EST message types. Clients should handle same-origin redirects securely, perform a new TLS security check for other origins, and recreate a CSR containing TLS channel-binding data when a redirect changes the TLS session.

feature_sentence: Expose EST operations through the standardized well-known URI paths
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ17. EST server paths begin under /.well-known/est and use operation suffixes such as /cacerts, /simpleenroll, /simplereenroll, /fullcmc, /serverkeygen, and /csrattrs. Additional labels may distinguish services while preserving the required operation paths.

feature_sentence: Enforce secure HTTP-based client authentication behavior
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ18. Servers may request HTTP Basic or Digest authentication in addition to, or when falling back from, TLS client authentication. These mechanisms must run over TLS 1.1 or later without NULL or anonymous cipher suites, and clients must not send authentication credentials to a server they have not authorized.

feature_sentence: Use the defined media types for each EST request and response message
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ19. Each EST operation uses the appropriate standardized HTTP Content-Type and media type for CA certificates, PKCS#10 enrollment requests, CMC responses, Full CMC messages, server-key-generation responses, and CSR attributes.

feature_sentence: Protect all EST communication with an authenticated TLS layer
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ20. EST communications must use HTTPS with TLS 1.1 or later, negotiate acceptable cipher suites, and provide the required mutual authentication behavior. The server is authenticated during the TLS handshake except for explicitly allowed bootstrap or Full CMC cases, and TLS channel binding must be supported for enrollment proof.

feature_sentence: Authenticate and authorize the EST server using TLS certificates
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ21. Certificate-based TLS server authentication must be supported. The client validates the server certificate according to PKI rules using explicit and, when enabled, implicit trust-anchor databases, preserves the distinction between those trust sources, and performs the corresponding authorization checks.

feature_sentence: Authenticate and authorize EST clients using TLS certificates when available
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ22. TLS client authentication is the recommended identification method and the server must support certificate-based client authentication. The server validates the client certificate, applies the appropriate trust-anchor databases, preserves explicit-versus-implicit trust semantics, and performs client authorization checks.

feature_sentence: Support secure certificate-less TLS mutual authentication for enrollment
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ23. When neither side uses certificates, the client and server may negotiate a certificate-less TLS suite. The mechanism must resist dictionary attacks and use a zero-knowledge-style protocol, such as suitable TLS-SRP suites, so successful authentication demonstrates knowledge of a shared secret.

feature_sentence: Require proof that the enrolling client possesses the requested private key
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ24. Enrollment requests provide proof-of-possession through a signature made with the private key corresponding to the requested public key. EST can strengthen this by binding the signed request to information from the authenticated TLS session.

feature_sentence: Bind client identity and proof-of-possession to the active TLS session
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ25. Clients should place TLS channel-binding information such as tls-unique into the signed certification request when linking identity and proof-of-possession. If supplied, the server must verify it and may reject requests that omit the binding when policy requires it.

feature_sentence: Authorize the EST server before accepting responses or sending credentials
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ26. The client must verify that the authenticated EST server is authorized before accepting server responses or answering HTTP authentication challenges. Authorization depends on whether explicit trust anchors, implicit trust anchors, or certificate-less authentication established the server identity.

feature_sentence: Validate server identity when using the client explicit trust-anchor database
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ27. When the server certificate is validated using an Explicit TA database, the client must verify the configured or redirected URI against the authenticated server identity according to the applicable identity rules, unless the certificate carries the designated CMC registration-authority usage.

feature_sentence: Validate server identity when using the client implicit trust-anchor database
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ28. When an Implicit TA database authenticates the EST server, the client must verify the configured URI and every redirect URI against the server identity. The authorized server is determined from the provisioned or most recent redirect URI together with the authenticated identity.

feature_sentence: Apply local CA policy when authorizing certificate issuance to clients
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ29. Certificate issuance is controlled by local CA policy represented by EST server configuration. The server can use the client's authenticated TLS identity and HTTP credentials when applying that policy and should recognize appropriately authorized registration-authority clients.

feature_sentence: Provide a function for distributing current CA certificates to clients
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ31. Clients can request a copy of the current CA certificate set, normally before performing other EST operations.

feature_sentence: Bootstrap an explicit trust-anchor database when no trusted CA is initially configured
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ32. A minimally configured client may temporarily complete an unauthenticated TLS connection only to retrieve bootstrap trust information, require out-of-band or human verification of the CA material, create an Explicit TA database from accepted data, and establish a new authenticated TLS session before any other EST exchange.

feature_sentence: Request current CA certificates through the /cacerts operation
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ33. Clients use HTTPS GET on /cacerts to obtain the EST CA trust-anchor information. Both clients and servers must support this function, clients should refresh CA information before it expires, and the client must authenticate and authorize the server or follow the defined bootstrap procedure.

feature_sentence: Return a valid CA certificate chain in a successful /cacerts response
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ34. A successful /cacerts response uses HTTP 200 and a certs-only CMC Simple PKI Response with the appropriate PKCS#7 media type and base64 transfer encoding. The response must contain the current root and any intermediate certificates needed to build the chain, and the client stores the accepted CA certificate as an explicit trust anchor.

feature_sentence: Support simple enrollment and re-enrollment certificate request operations
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ35. Clients request new certificates with POST /simpleenroll and renew or rekey certificates with POST /simplereenroll, both of which servers must support. Client and server authentication, authorization, CA-certificate validation, and submitted TLS channel-binding information must be checked before issuance.

feature_sentence: Submit a properly signed PKCS#10 request for simple enrollment
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ36. POST /simpleenroll carries a Simple PKI Request containing a PKCS#10 CSR using the required media type and transfer encoding. The CSR signature provides proof-of-possession, subject changes may be requested through the appropriate attribute, and clients may request additional certificates while authenticating with an existing one.

feature_sentence: Renew or rekey a certificate through the simple re-enrollment operation
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ37. POST /simplereenroll uses the same request format as simple enrollment. Subject and SubjectAltName normally remain identical to the current certificate unless an authorized change is requested; retaining the public key performs renewal, while changing it performs rekeying.

feature_sentence: Handle successful, failed, and pending simple enrollment responses correctly
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ38. Successful enrollment returns HTTP 200 with a certs-only PKCS#7 response containing the issued certificate. Failures use suitable 4xx/5xx status codes and explanatory error data, while HTTP 202 indicates pending processing and requires Retry-After handling and a repeated request after the specified delay.

feature_sentence: Support the optional Full CMC certificate request operation
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ39. Clients may request certificates using HTTPS POST to /fullcmc. Full CMC support is optional for both clients and servers.

feature_sentence: Validate and correctly encode Full CMC requests
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ40. A POST to /fullcmc must contain a valid Full PKI Request. Invalid requests are rejected, while valid requests use the defined PKCS#7 CMC-request media type and base64 transfer encoding.

feature_sentence: Return the appropriate Full CMC success or error response
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ41. Successful Full CMC enrollment returns HTTP 200 with either a certs-only Simple PKI Response or Full PKI Response in the defined PKCS#7 media type. Rejected requests use 4xx or 5xx status codes and include a CMC error response where required.

feature_sentence: Generate and securely return a private key and certificate on server request
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ42. POST /serverkeygen may request server-side generation of a private key and associated certificate. Client and server authentication and authorization are required, NULL-confidentiality suites are forbidden, and the TLS protection used to return the generated key must provide confidentiality appropriate to the key.

feature_sentence: Use the requested asymmetric key identifier when encrypting a server-generated private key
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ45. A client requesting asymmetric protection for a server-generated private key includes an AsymmetricDecryptKeyIdentifier. The server must terminate the request if it cannot locate a matching public key, and the selected key must be suitable for the required key transport or key agreement use.

feature_sentence: Return server-generated key material in a protected multipart response
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ46. Successful server-side key generation returns HTTP 200 with multipart/mixed content containing a private-key part and certificate part. Unprotected private keys use the specified PKCS#8 encoding; when additional protection is requested, CMS signing and enveloping are used with key-management details appropriate to the selected symmetric or asymmetric protection key.

feature_sentence: Allow clients to discover CA-required or desired CSR attributes
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ47. Because CA policy may require certificate-request attributes unknown to the client, clients should request the expected CSR attributes before enrollment when appropriate. The server should not normally require authentication or authorization merely to answer this attribute-discovery request.

feature_sentence: Request CSR attribute requirements through the /csrattrs operation
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ48. The client obtains the CA's desired certification-request attributes by sending an HTTPS GET request to the EST server at the /csrattrs operation path.

feature_sentence: Return CSR attributes using the defined status codes and encoding
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ49. When policy permits a CSR Attributes Response, the server returns HTTP 200 and encodes zero or more requested OIDs or attributes as application/csrattrs with base64 transfer encoding. HTTP 204 or 404 indicates that no response is available, and clients ignore unrecognized attributes.

feature_sentence: Use the standardized EST URI and media-type registrations
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ50. This benchmark artifact captures the IANA registrations associated with EST, including the well-known 'est' URI suffix, application media types, and the registered object identifier used by the protocol.

feature_sentence: Apply EST security safeguards for credentials, trust anchors, and authentication
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ51. EST implementations must account for the risks of Basic authentication, implicit trust anchors, certificate-less authentication, channel binding, and credential exposure. The guidance favors one-time bootstrap credentials, careful trust-anchor management, secure authentication suites, and identity/POP linking to reduce impersonation and forwarding attacks.

feature_sentence: Use the normative standards referenced by the EST specification
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ52. This artifact is the specification's normative-reference section rather than a behavioral feature. It is retained because the official LibEST traceability benchmark models it as a requirement artifact and links it to implementation/test artifacts.

feature_sentence: Retain the informative standards and background references used by EST
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ53. This artifact contains informative references used by the EST specification. It is not itself a functional behavior, but it is retained unchanged at the artifact level because it belongs to the official LibEST benchmark requirement set.

feature_sentence: Support the documented /cacerts exchange behavior
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ55. This artifact provides a concrete example of a valid /cacerts exchange, including the initial TLS interaction, HTTPS GET request, and expected protocol framing. It is retained as a benchmark requirement/example artifact for traceability.

feature_sentence: Support the documented /csrattrs exchange behavior
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ56. This artifact gives a concrete valid /csrattrs exchange in which the client authenticates with an existing CA-issued certificate and sends the expected HTTPS GET request. It is retained as a benchmark requirement/example artifact for traceability.

feature_sentence: Support the documented simple enrollment and re-enrollment exchange behavior
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ57. This artifact provides an example /simpleenroll exchange and notes that /simplereenroll is similar. It demonstrates HTTP authentication challenge behavior, TLS use, and the enrollment POST flow and is retained as a benchmark requirement/example artifact.

feature_sentence: Support the documented server-key-generation exchange behavior
documentation_text: Native LibEST RQ58. This artifact provides a concrete /serverkeygen example using an authenticated client, TLS, an HTTPS POST, PKCS#10 content, and the expected response framing. It is retained as a benchmark requirement/example artifact for traceability.
